item.title: History Language Models
item.description: Training Language Models on Curated Datasets
item.dc:creator: Niclas Griesshaber
item.content:encoded:
This post builds on our paper “A Language Model from 1913: Pretraining on Historical Text”, accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Main Conference and co-authored by Xiaoxi Luo, Zachary Shinnick, Niclas Griesshaber, Yixuan Wang, Junchi Yu, Freda Shi, Philip Torr, and Yao Lu.

In this post, we 1) explain what History Language Models are and explore some of their applications, 2) describe the challenges we faced in creating TypewriterLM, our own History Language Model, and 3) discuss what may help advance this emerging field.

1) History Language Models and their Applications

Why do we not simply prompt a modern large language model (LLM) to imagine it is in 1913? Because it has already learned about what happened after 1913 during training. It cannot unlearn what it has seen, even if we ask it to pretend otherwise.

By contrast, the defining feature of History Language Models is that they are designed to be trained only on texts published before a “historical” cutoff date. For example, our TypewriterLM has a cutoff date of 1913. Some examples of what this could enable for historical research and AI for Science include:

  • Retrospective Forecasting: We could ask a History Language Model with a 1913 cutoff: “Do you think there will soon be a major war in Europe?”

  • Historical Decision-Making: Instead of asking the model to predict what happens next, we could give it new information and ask how it would respond at a turning point in history: “You are the British Prime Minister. Germany has just invaded Luxembourg. What options do you consider and what course of action will you take?” This would be particularly interesting with models whose training data could be tailored to a specific historical situation. For example, we could train a History Language Model exclusively on British texts published up to 1913 and then fine-tune it on material from the British Prime Minister, such as his public speeches, to make the model better reflect his language and views.

  • Text-as-Data Applications with Historical Priors: Modern LLMs are already being used to classify or score historical texts. For example, they can measure how much fear is expressed in newspaper articles from 1913. These scores can then be used to construct a fear index over time. But modern LLMs may interpret fear differently from readers in 1913. Comparing their scores with those of History Language Models could reveal how the same newspaper articles may have been interpreted differently in the past, as present-day knowledge and values may shape our reading of historical documents.

  • The AGI Einstein Test: An unreleased OpenAI model has produced a proposed solution to a Millennium Prize Problem. But could an AI system also make a conceptual leap as big as Einstein’s theory of general relativity using only the information available to him before his breakthrough in 1915?

2) Challenges in Training History Language Models

In our paper, we presented a small number of qualitative examples related to the applications discussed above.

Experimenting with TypewriterLM suggested that more capable History Language Models will be needed before these applications become reliable and useful. Scaling these models further will therefore be necessary, but it will also amplify several of the challenges we encountered when training our 7-billion-parameter TypewriterLM.

Scarcity of Machine-Readable Historical Text Data

Historical texts are not born digital. They first have to be brought from the physical into the digital world by scanning them into formats such as PDFs or image files. Digital libraries then use optical character recognition (OCR) to extract the text into machine-readable formats such as .txt or XML files. For our pretraining corpus, we collected several such datasets that were already available online in a machine-readable form. But the amount of historical text available in this form is still much smaller than the amount of digital text used to train modern LLMs.

Data Leakage in the Historical Pretraining Dataset

The defining feature of History Language Models is that they should only be trained on data from before the cutoff date. But the historical datasets we collected from digital archives can contain errors, for example incorrect publication dates in the metadata. At the scale of billions of tokens, it is impossible to manually check every document to verify that it was actually published before the cutoff date. This makes it very difficult to guarantee that no post-1913 information entered the pretraining dataset. To reduce this risk, we built a filtering pipeline to remove potential sources of leakage from our historical pretraining corpus. In the end, our pretraining corpus consisted of 54 billion historical tokens.

Data Leakage When Teaching the Model to Follow Instructions

Once TypewriterLM had been pretrained on the collected historical datasets, we still had to teach it to answer questions. Pretraining teaches a language model to predict the next token, which allows it to continue sentences, but not to answer questions.

To teach the model some degree of instruction-following, we needed a separate dataset of question-answer pairs for supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Such datasets are relatively scarce in historical sources, so we used Claude to help generate the instructions. This creates another potential source of leakage: even when the SFT dataset is grounded in historical source texts, modern wording or framing may bias the model through the generated instructions.

Compute

Constructing the pretraining and SFT datasets was the foundation, but turning them into a 7-billion-parameter language model required massive compute.

Our academic institutions did not have enough computing capacity to train the model from scratch. Therefore, we applied for external compute and were fortunate to receive access to Isambard-AI, the UK’s most powerful AI supercomputer, hosted by the Bristol Centre for Supercomputing at the University of Bristol.

Benchmarking and Evaluation

Two important dimensions for evaluating History Language Models are their general capability and whether they have learned information from after the cutoff date. Both are difficult to evaluate.

Standard benchmarks are designed for modern LLMs and may favour them because they use modern language and contexts. Therefore, we filtered HellaSwag to remove modern topics and created another version rewritten in historical language. The results showed that a temporal mismatch in language style can itself affect benchmark performance.

We also evaluated whether TypewriterLM had learned information from after 1913 by asking whether it knew major historical events from before and after the cutoff date. We simply measured whether it could recall these events. This evaluation is also only meaningful if the model can reliably recall events before the cutoff date. Otherwise, failure to recall a post-cutoff event could simply reflect poor recall in general rather than the absence of leakage. A separate limitation is that leakage can take the form of any information contained in the training data and may therefore escape a fixed evaluation benchmark.

3) What Could Help Advance the Field

Working Directly with Archives

Physical archives store much more historical text than is currently available in machine-readable form. The US National Archives alone holds billions of pages, but estimates that less than 4% of its physical collection has been scanned.

Of these scans, only a fraction is likely to have been converted into machine-readable text that is readily available for training History Language Models.

The first bottleneck is scanning. Old historical books often have to be restored and prepared before they can be scanned, which can be very expensive. In addition, the scanning process itself is slow because these books are often valuable and must be handled carefully to avoid any damage.

The second bottleneck is converting these scans into machine-readable text. Historical documents vary in fonts, layouts, languages, and handwriting. Because of this heterogeneity, converting historical documents into machine-readable text remains difficult at scale. Frontier vision-language models can now achieve expert-human-level performance on some English historical handwriting and can handle many difficult historical documents, but applying them to enough pages to build a pretraining corpus of billions of tokens would still be prohibitively expensive.

Working directly with archives could therefore create value at two levels. At scale, many such datasets could provide the large amounts of historical text needed to train more capable History Language Models. At the same time, each dataset created from an individual primary source could be highly valuable to historians studying the specific topic, place, institution, or period it covers.

Building an Open Community Around Historical Datasets

Digital archives could make more of their machine-readable historical datasets openly available on platforms such as Hugging Face.

This would allow researchers to combine datasets from different archives to train larger History Language Models. An open community could also help improve these datasets over time by identifying and removing data leakage, correcting metadata, and improving the underlying OCR text if both images and transcriptions are uploaded.

Curating Tightly Controlled Datasets at Scale

Critics may argue that History Language Models will never work as intended because it is impossible to completely control what information enters the training dataset at scale. Even the smallest amount of leakage could matter. For example, in the AGI Einstein Test, even a tiny hint of later knowledge could help the model come up with the theory of general relativity and would therefore create a false positive.

But tightly controlling what information enters the training dataset at scale does not seem to be an inherently unsolvable problem. Frontier LLMs could already be used to go through historical datasets and identify documents that were published after the cutoff date because of incorrect metadata or other errors. They could also flag documents containing concepts or vocabulary that should not appear before the specified cutoff date. This suggests that the problem is tractable. The main challenge is developing a much cheaper filtering pipeline that can operate at scale while being equally or even more effective.

More broadly, controlling what information enters the pretraining corpus at scale is becoming a recognised research direction in machine learning. For example, researchers from Tübingen and Zürich created LittleLearner, a language model trained on a curated corpus designed to exclude “concepts, facts, and vocabulary taught above Grade 5” — essentially a child LLM.

History Language Models may therefore be understood as a subfield within a broader research area that trains language models on tightly controlled training datasets.

Pooling GPU and Data Resources

Several research groups have been working on History Language Models. As these models have to scale to become more useful for the applications discussed at the beginning, their demand for compute will also increase. Academic institutions are often compute-constrained, which limits how quickly these models can be scaled.

One way forward could therefore be to pool GPU resources across research groups working on History Language Models to train larger and more capable models.

Frontier AI labs may also find this area interesting from an interpretability or even commercial perspective. Collaborations between frontier labs, historians, and digital archives could provide the compute and data needed to push this field much further.

History Language Models could then become artefacts that historians study, while history could also help us better understand the limitations of AI.

item.title: From dusty scans to one chart: how we traced industrial self-generation in Spain, 1958–1966
item.description: A behind-the-scenes look at archival data work, done in partnership with the Chronos: The AI Co-Historian.
item.dc:creator: Mar_Rubio-Varas
item.content:encoded:
This guest article is by Mar Rubio-Varas, Professor of Economic History in the Department of Economics at the Universidad Pública de Navarra (UPNA) and a research fellow at the Institute for Advanced Research in Business and Economics (INARBE), currently Research Fellow at Clare Hall and the Faculty of History, University of Cambridge.

If you want to understand the modernization of an economy, follow the power lines. We recently set out to answer a highly specific question about mid-century Spain: how much of the electricity used by Spanish industry was self-generated (produced by autoproductoras) versus bought from the public grid (servicio público)? And more importantly, how did that split evolve as the country industrialized from the late 1950s onward? It’s a timely question. Self-consumption is being blamed for pushing up costs on both sides of the Atlantic (here, here and here), and energy economists are split: some want more self-generation, others want to cut it down and its subsidies scrapped for good. But industrial electricity self-consumption is nothing new. Alcoa’s aluminum smelters at Niagara Falls started out in 1895 as the local hydro utility’s very first customer, and within little more than a decade the company was building its own power plants to feed them. Who should generate, and who should pay for the grid everyone else still needs: it’s a fight that’s well over a century old.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

The answer lived inside a single statistical table hidden in old electricity statistics in Spain. The problem was that we didn’t know how far through time this table survived, where it sat in each annual yearbook, or if the data could even be extracted without months of manual transcription.

Here is how we turned a massive, heterogeneous archive into a single, clean historical narrative using a mix of traditional historical sleuthing and AI.

The Archival Minefield

Our raw material was the annual Estadística de la Industria de la Energía Eléctrica, published by Spain’s Ministry of Industry (today MITECO), starting in 1958. These are publicly available online.

As a corpus, it is a veritable museum of document technology spanning 60 years. The manifest listed roughly 199 files found online, with a real data payload of 87 PDFs, 29 spreadsheets, and 19 archives. Tracking a single table through this collection meant navigating three distinct eras of data storage:

  1. 1958–1993: Scanned PDFs of printed books. These are images only, with no searchable text. They feature landscape tables rotated 90 degrees and old-school apostrophe-style decimals (e.g., 6’31).

  2. 1994–2012: ZIP archives containing fixed-width plain-text tables that are beautifully machine-readable.

  3. 2013–2024: ODS spreadsheets and born-digital PDFs with a flawless text layer.

The same table changes format, filename, layout, and even statistical definition across the decades. We needed a pipeline that could handle all of it. Luckily, Lorenz Hufe and Niclas Griesshaber have created Chronos: The AI Co-Historian, and came to UPNA to explain it in a hands-on workshop for our economic history group. Here is what I achieved in one morning.

The Workflow: AI meets the Historian

Phase 1: Local Triage (The Cheap Work)
Before throwing expensive AI models at the problem, we inventoried and classified every file using simple, local Python scripts. We used basic file triage, unzip, text extraction, and regular expressions to determine page counts and distinguish scanned documents from text-searchable ones. This work quickly confirmed that from 1994 onward, the table was already plain text, and it ran continuously until 2015 (later renamed to “energía distribuida/comercializada por sectores”). It also told us exactly which early years would require heavy image processing.

Phase 2: The Human Skim
For the scanned 1958–1969 books, the cheapest and most reliable “table detector” isn’t an algorithm—it’s a historian. Instead of letting an AI blindly scan 4,000 pages, a human skimmed the volumes and recorded a simple one-line reference for each year: year | file | PDF page | short title.

This step paid immediate dividends. We discovered that the 1959 and 1960 target table was absent from the original scan (someone forgot to scan those pages, it should be somewhere in the paper copy).

Phase 3: Render and Read
With the exact pages flagged, we set up a fully local pipeline. We used PyMuPDF to render the target PDF pages into crisp 300-dpi images, and Tesseract (loaded with Spanish and old-orthography models) for a free, first-pass OCR.

Only the final, flagged table images were sent to the AI vision model. The AI is remarkably adept at reading faint, comma-decimal tables that trip up standard OCR. For each page, Chronos returned a structured, machine-readable record: sector label, public-service MWh, self-producer MWh, total MWh, and the printed percentage.

Phase 4: Paranoia and Verification
Never trust the first read. We cross-checked the local OCR against the vision model’s output and subjected every table to strict arithmetic validation. The sector rows had to sum to the printed total, and within each row, the equation was absolute: public service + self-producers = total.

This mathematical paranoia caught real errors. Two cells in 1963 and one in 1961 had been misread by the models. In each case, the printed percentage column acted as our tie-breaker. If a value read as 3.11% in one column and 4.60% in another, we could reverse-engineer exactly which digit the AI had hallucinated. After these corrections, all seven comparable years reconciled to the exact megawatt-hour.

During this verification, we also uncovered a genuine methodology break in 1967. The Ministry switched from a lettered list of industrial uses (subscribers over 50 kW) to a broader, numbered list of all consumer sectors. Because the two aren’t directly comparable, we treated them as separate blocks, choosing to focus exclusively on the clean 1958–1966 industrial series for our initial analysis. We also had to explicitly map a subtle 1962 reclassification (the sudden insertion of an Irrigation row) so the sectors lined up perfectly across the decade.

The Payoff: What the Data Shows

Once the verified records were consolidated into a long-format dataset and a sector-by-year matrix, the historical narrative finally emerged (all within the same conversation in Chronos AI!)

Between 1958 and 1966, Spanish industrial self-generation almost doubled in absolute terms, climbing from approximately 1.0 to 1.9 million MWh. Yet, despite this massive investment in private generators, self-generation’s share of total industrial consumption fell steadily from about 13% to 10%.

The takeaway is clear: while industry kept building its own capacity to keep the lights on, grid supply from the public-service utilities was growing even faster. Throughout the 1960s, Spanish industry was progressively, and permanently, electrifying from the public grid.

Next step will be to continue using Chronos up to 2024, to figure out whether industrial self-consumption in Spain follows a U-shaped trend rather than a continued decline over time, identify the sectors more prompt to self-consumption and try to understand how that has changed over time. But none of this would have been possible without Chronos, The AI Co-Historian, specifically designed for economic history tasks. A whole new set of questions can now be answered with data that already existed, but that was impossible for humans alone to handle.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

item.title: Mapping Frankfurt's Merchants of 1812 using AI
item.description: An exemplary demonstration of how Chronos can enhance historical research.
item.dc:creator: Lorenz Hufe
item.content:encoded:
Chronos - The AI Co-Historian

Working with an archive is, for the most part, an exercise in patience. A single volume can hold several hundred pages of blackletter type or handwriting, and the facts a researcher actually wants - who lived where, which goods were traded in what house and so on - sit across thousands of short, near-identical entries. Reading them is slow and turning them into structured data which you can sort, count, or place on a map is even slower, and honestly: it is the kind of work that often never gets finished.

To take on that mechanical labour without taking over the scholarship behind it we built Chronos: The AI Co-Historian. It is an AI agent that sits alongside a historian and does the boring parts of the job: converting scanned page into structured records, finding streets on old maps, and cross-reference entries across different sources. Chronos does not replace the researcher’s judgement but unlocks a smoother way of interaction with the primary sources.

A real concern when using AI for historical applications is that the models misread old type, quietly invent plausible-looking details, and fabricate complete sections. Rather than hiding that, we deisgned Chronos around it. Every record produced by Chronos can be traced back to the exact bounding box of the scan it came from. When the agent reports e.g. that a wine merchant named Abendantz traded in the Papagaygasse, it can show you the exact position in the primary source that says so - allowing you to inspect and correct potential errors. This design makes the collaboration between Chronos and you interactive and trustworthy: you can always check the work against the page in the split of a second.

In the rest of this article we will demonstrate a small scale demo project from beginning to end, because the easiert way to explain Chronos is to show how you can work with it.

The merchant register and the map

The project begins with two scans, both digitised by the Universitätsbibliothek Johann Christian Senckenberg in Frankfurt.

The first is the Handlungs-Adreß-Kalender von Frankfurt am Main auf das Jahr 1812, a commercial address calendar of the kind most German cities printed each year. It is part almanac, part business directory, part postal timetable, and it runs to 168 scanned pages set in Fraktur. At its heart is an alphabetical list of the city's merchants and manufacturers. Each entry is terse: a name, a street, and a phrase describing what the person dealt in.

The second is the Geometrischer Grundriss von Frankfurt am Mayn, an engraved city plan from 1811. It is a single sheet so finely worked that the scan measures nearly eleven thousand pixels across. It names hundreds of streets, squares, inns, gates and churches directly on the plan, and a legend divides the city into fourteen quarters.

Put side by side, the two sources almost ask to be joined. The directory knows who traded what, and gives an address; the map knows where those addresses actually are. Neither, on its own, can show you the geography of commerce in the city, but together they can reveal meaningful insights.

Reading the directory

The first thing we usually do when analyzing a book with Chronos, is to get a rough overview over the source. So we instructed Chronos to get an overview of the trader directory it sampled pages across the volume. Chronos then spawns many sub-agents that follow Chronos’s prompt to describe a single page each.

Based on these summaries Chronos reads through the book, sampling across sections rather than reading every page. Using this method Chronos reconstructed the table of contents of our commercial address book and, just as importantly, the page numbering. The first few pages are unpaginated, but once the printed page numbers begin they sit a fixed distance from the scan numbers, until later in the book a couple of unnumbered insert leaves slip in.

This is the resulting table of contents:

Now that we know that the interesting pages are scans 35-86 we can start extracting entries. Looking at the first page we can observe a clear structure. Every entry has a name, street and a description of the wares they sell.

Then we instruct Chronos to these entries of every page using a specific json schema:

{
  "name":          "Johann Valentin Albert",
  "street":        "in der Döngesgasse, am Liebfrauenberg",
  "house_number":  null,
  "quarter":       null,
  "trade":         "mit Galanterie= Kunst= und Spielwaaren, en gros und en détail …",
  "raw_text":      "Johann Valentin Albert, in der Döngesgasse, …",
  "page":          35,
  "printed_page":  1,
  "bbox":          { "x":0.14, "y":0.31, "w":0.72, "h":0.06 }
}

The schema does two jobs. Firstly it tells the model precisely what to pull out of these sixty pages. Secondly it carries the bbox property - the position of the entry on the page, in fractions of the page's width and height - which is what later lets any record be shown back on its source. The bounding box is what introduces provenance into the system. Using the specialized data viewer in Chronos you can easily jump to each image crop to verify if the retrieved data is correct.

Chronos worked all pages in parallel and extracted the 871 entries. The outcome still required some post processing, because the merchant’s entries occasionally ran over a page break, so its final line appears at the very top of the next scan, but after a few messages back and forth Chronos solved this issue as well, fixing broken entires across the break, so that e.g. Fahr-thor became Fahrthor again.

What the directory can now tell us

Once the merchants are structured records rather than printed lines, you can start asking the source questions. The simplest is also the most revealing: what did these people actually trade in? Chronos sorted each entry’s description into eighteen broad categories. Setting aside the entries that name no goods at all, the commercial character of the city comes through clearly.

Textiles dominate, and by a wide margin - cloth and silk together account for more dealers than the next two categories combined, which fits Frankfurt’s long standing as a textile market. Behind them sit the colonial-goods grocers, dealing in spices, coffee and sugar, then the wine trade. The category that rewards a second look is the cluster of bankers and bill-brokers: fifty firms whose business was money rather than goods, an early glimpse of the financial city Frankfurt would become.

Where they clustered

A second question is geographic even before any map is involved: where were these businesses? Sorting the same records by street shows how tightly commerce concentrated.

A handful of lanes - the Fahrgasse, the Döngesgasse, the Schnurgasse - hold far more merchants than anywhere else, seeming to be the hot spots for traders.

Placing the merchants on the 1811 map

Georeferencing usually means assigning a real-world latitude and longitude. Here goal is narrower: we want to place each merchant at the right spot on the 1811 map.

The difficulty is that the map does not come with a search function - after all its just a picture. So the first task was to build that missing index - a gazetteer.

Chronos cut the enormous sheet into a grid of tiles small enough for a vision model to read carefully, and worked through them one at a time, recording every label it could find together with its position. The result was a catalogue of 456 named features - 147 streets, but also squares, inns, gates, churches and individual buildings - each tied to a coordinate on the plan.

Matching the directory’s addresses to that catalogue sounds straight forward but is full of small traps. The same street appears as Mainzergasse in the directory and Mayntzer Gasse on the map; addresses arrive wrapped in prepositions and house-sign names, as in “in der Döngesgasse, am Liebfrauenberg”; the long ſ and the ß have to be normalised before strings can be compared. Chronos worked it way from exact matches outward to looser ones - prefix, then substring, then fuzzy similarity - and kept a hand-curated table of known aliases so that spelling variants did not silently get dropped.

Loose matching, though, is where a pipeline like this can start halucinating, so every placement was checked again. For each located street Chronos took a tight crop around the proposed spot, looked again, and nudged the point onto the centre of the actual label. The verification pass earned its keep: one entry had matched the “Berg” buried inside Römer Berg and landed in the wrong place entirely, and then was thrown out. Repeated close-up passes also settled a more deflating truth - that the smallest lanes, the Borngasse and the Kruggasse and a dozen others, are simply not labelled on the 1811 sheet, however hard one looks.

In the end 468 merchants were placed and confirmed - about four in five of the entries that had a usable address - alongside twenty locations drawn from the postal section. The hundred or so that remain unplaced are less failures of effort than honest gaps: streets the engraver never named, or entries that gave a house sign and no street at all. Plotted all together, the located merchants trace the same commercial spine the street counts had hinted at, now as visible geography.

Building something a historian can use

A dataset that lives only in a JSON file is quite hard validate. The last thing Chronos did was turn the results into a small web application, overlaying the geo-located traders, the original source crops and the map.

Go ahead and check the website out for yourself if you want!

If this blog post motivated you to learn more about Chronos, that’s great! You can find the open-source code on our Github (make sure to leave a ⭐) or join our Discord if you have any questions.

Every Tuesday at 11:00 am CEST, and are available for questions on Discord are available for Q&A, installation help, and general discussions about AI for history.
